package_info.package_manager: custom firmware (Linux-based, not a standard package manager)
package_info.package_versions: unspecified; affected versions use Linux kernel EOL 2016 and packages up to 23 years old
package_info.why_malicious: The firmware is not intentionally malicious, but it is dangerously insecure due to the inclusion of extremely outdated Linux kernel versions and bundled software packages with hundreds of known, unpatched vulnerabilities. This exposes systems to a high risk of compromise and is considered grossly negligent from a security perspective, as attackers can exploit well-documented flaws.

behavioral_signatures: Firmware includes Linux kernel versions that reached end-of-life before 2017, indicating lack of security updates.
Bundling of software components (e.g., OpenSSL, Apache, BusyBox) with known CVEs older than 10 years.
Absence of a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) or any transparency regarding included software versions.
Presence of default or hardcoded credentials in configuration files (if identified in firmware analysis).
file_indicators: Firmware images containing Linux kernel binaries with version strings indicating EOL status (e.g., 2.6.x, 3.0.x).
Presence of software binaries or libraries (e.g., openssl, apache, busybox) with version metadata matching known vulnerable releases.
Lack of SBOM or manifest files in firmware image.
Configuration files with default or hardcoded credentials (e.g., /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, or custom config files).
network_indicators: No direct network indicators; risk arises from exploitation of known vulnerabilities in exposed services (e.g., SSH, web admin interface, VPN endpoints) present in the firmware.
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Perform static analysis of firmware images to extract kernel and software component versions. Cross-reference all identified versions against public CVE databases to enumerate known vulnerabilities. Flag firmware images that lack an SBOM or manifest, or that contain kernel/software versions past end-of-life, as high risk. Additionally, scan for default or hardcoded credentials in configuration files. Automated tools should alert on any firmware image containing unsupported or unpatched components, or lacking transparency about included software.
